article_title: New Mexico Community Schools: Improving Student Opportunities and Outcomes
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief
title: New Mexico's six key practices framework for community schools
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department's community schools framework identifies six site-level practices for implementation: collaborative leadership, shared power, and voice; powerful student and family engagement; rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction; expanded, culturally enriched learning opportunities; a culture of belonging, safety, and care; and integrated systems of support. The brief states these practices are "grounded in research and the expertise of community school practitioners participating in the national Community Schools Forward task force" and were integrated into the strategic vision and daily operation of the profiled schools.
requirements: State implementation grants and a full-time community school coordinator at each school to pursue the practices
constraints: Practices must be tailored to the local school community, per the brief's statement that integrated implementation is "tailored to the local school community"
target_learners: K-12 students in New Mexico public schools
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, engagement, attendance, and academic achievement
examples: The three profiled districts (Albuquerque, Peñasco, Roswell) integrated the six practices into school transformation efforts supported by PED implementation grants.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief

article_title: New Mexico Community Schools: Improving Student Opportunities and Outcomes
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief
title: New Mexico community schools grant program and funding structure
description: New Mexico's Community Schools Act (2013, updated 2019) established a state grant program; legislative funding began in 2019 with an initial $2 million and totals $36.9 million allocated through 2025. For 2024-25, "90 schools either received funding for implementation grants or were designated to participate in the Accredit Community Schools pilot program." The program funds full-time community school coordinators, planning, and implementation, supplemented by federal Full-Service Community Schools grants totaling $7.5 million and a $1.8 million congressionally directed technical assistance award.
requirements: State appropriation and PED grant management and technical assistance infrastructure
constraints: The 2024 appropriation was reduced from $10 million to $8 million, with grant awards lowered accordingly
target_learners: Students in participating New Mexico public schools
target_learning_goals: Whole-child development and improved student opportunities and outcomes
examples: Table 1 lists annual appropriations from $2 million (2020) to $10 million (2024) and corresponding planning, implementation, and improvement grant awards.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief

article_title: New Mexico Community School Profile: Los Padillas Elementary School
citation: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief
title: New Mexico's six key site-level practices of community schools
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department defines a community school as "a whole child, comprehensive strategy to transform schools" where educators, families, community members, and students organize in- and out-of-school resources so young people thrive. PED identifies six key site-level practices grounded in research and practitioner expertise: expanded culturally enriched learning opportunities; rigorous community-connected classroom instruction; a culture of belonging, safety, and care; integrated systems of support; powerful student and family engagement; and collaborative leadership with shared power and voice. Los Padillas's transformation is organized around these practices.
requirements: Trusting relationships among school community members
constraints: Programs and services vary according to local context
target_learners: Whole-school student populations, including English learners and low-income communities
target_learning_goals: Student thriving, attendance, engagement, behavior, and academic outcomes
examples: Los Padillas implemented the practices through dual language instruction, the wildlife sanctuary, Genius Hour, wraparound services, and a Community School Council sharing decision-making.
key_sources: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief

description: The New Mexico Public Education Department defines a community school as "a whole child, comprehensive strategy to transform schools" where educators, families, community members, and students organize in- and out-of-school resources so young people thrive. article_title: Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis.
citation: Guan Cheng Ye, Chun Ping Liu, Wei Li, Hua Chao Zhu, Liu Lv, Zhen Hong Zhu, Yong Hong Wang, Jie Hu, Xiao Jia Zheng, Jing Ying Fang, Yu Cao Ma, Ming Xuan Liu, Yi Wen Wang, Ying Kai Gao, Zi Yu Zhang, Lu Ming Zhao, Cun Xiang Xie, Min Yee Lim, Hai Long Wang. (2025). Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07020-1
title: Network meta-analysis framework for ranking multiple teaching methods simultaneously
description: Network meta-analysis (NMA) is presented as "a new type of meta-analysis, which can compare the effectiveness of multiple interventions more intuitively and in detail, while traditional meta-analysis can only compare them in pairs". The article applies it with Stata 16.0's mvmeta package, using SMDs for continuous outcomes and ORs for binary outcomes, SUCRA curves to rank treatments probabilistically, node-splitting for inconsistency, and a league table for pairwise comparisons. It integrates direct and indirect evidence across 13 interventions.
requirements: Requires a connected network of comparative studies; interventions published in fewer than 3 literatures were excluded
constraints: Results are considered statistically insignificant if the 95% CI includes 1; heterogeneity was assessed via prediction intervals and node-splitting
target_learning_goals: comparative effectiveness evaluation of teaching methods
examples: The article ranked 13 teaching methods using SUCRA, with PBL + WeChat first for theoretical scores (88%) and PBL + CP first for medical record scores (99.9%)

(2025). Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07020-1

article_title: Exploring core competence in first-year medical students through narrative medicine and peer-assisted learning: a mixed-methods study.
citation: Lin Peixin, Yin Xiaolin, Zheng Xuankun, He Sijia, Cai Yuexin, Deng Xiaozheng, Chen Tongtong, Liang Weiquan, Liang Suqiong, Liang Yuanke, Lu Yiwen, Lin Haoyu. (2026). Exploring core competence in first-year medical students through narrative medicine and peer-assisted learning: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10160-7
title: The integrated NM-PAL curriculum pattern: five synergistic modules combining narrative cases with small-group peer mentoring
description: The NM-PAL model integrated senior medical students (recruited from the top 30% of their class, given 10 hours of training, and supervised via weekly debriefing) as peer mentors within a reciprocal learning community. The curriculum consisted of "five synergistic modules: in-depth NM-case reading, case discussions, medical terminology acquisition, doctor-patient role-playing, and academic presentations," totalling 30 instruction hours, delivered in small classes of 6–8 students versus lecture-based classes of 30–40.
requirements: Senior peer mentors recruited based on academic performance, prior teaching experience, and communication skills
A standardized teaching protocol and weekly faculty debriefing sessions with mentors
constraints: Both groups completed the same total formal contact hours and curriculum objectives
Benefits are sensitive to the perceived expertise of the peer mentors
target_learning_goals: Contextualized clinical competence and early professional identity formation
key_sources: Lin Peixin, Yin Xiaolin, Zheng Xuankun, He Sijia, Cai Yuexin, Deng Xiaozheng, Chen Tongtong, Liang Weiquan, Liang Suqiong, Liang Yuanke, Lu Yiwen, Lin Haoyu. (2026). Exploring core competence in first-year medical students through narrative medicine and peer-assisted learning: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10160-7

article_title: Practical Exploration of Medical Students' Curriculum Education Model in the Context of New Medical Science-Taking Biochemistry and Molecular Biology as an Example.
citation: Xu Shuzi, Chen Yiyang, and Wu Juanjuan. (2025). Practical Exploration of Medical Students' Curriculum Education Model in the Context of New Medical Science—Taking Biochemistry and Molecular Biology as an Example. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education 53, no. 6: 647–655. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.70019
title: New Medical Science biochemistry course reform pattern: online–offline blended learning plus flipped classroom with student 'little teachers' plus humanistic-ethical case integration
description: A course-level instructional pattern for biochemistry and molecular biology tailored to China's New Medical Science initiative, combining three strategies the authors describe as serving "knowledge application + competency development + value shaping". Pre-class online modules let students master foundations independently; in-class sessions apply knowledge to clinical scenarios; students act as "little teachers" presenting key concepts while teachers coach and target gaps; small-group case analyses link scientific content to ethical reasoning (e.g., COVID-19 resource allocation dilemmas, Nobel laureate research journeys).
requirements: Pre-class online modules (e.g., MOOCs) students can complete independently before in-class application sessions
Instructors willing to shift from lecture delivery to coaching, observing presentations to identify knowledge gaps
Case materials linking biochemical content to ethical and clinical scenarios
constraints: The authors note learning effectiveness depends greatly on students' active learning attitude and self-study abilities; less motivated or less confident students need more teacher assistance
target_learners: first-year undergraduate medical students (stomatology and clinical medicine)
target_learning_goals: biochemistry and molecular biology knowledge and application
examples: Stomatology cohorts 2020–2022 at Nantong University implemented the new mode within the new-medicine framework while clinical medicine cohorts kept traditional multimedia lecture teaching
key_sources: Xu Shuzi, Chen Yiyang, and Wu Juanjuan. (2025). Practical Exploration of Medical Students' Curriculum Education Model in the Context of New Medical Science—Taking Biochemistry and Molecular Biology as an Example. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education 53, no. 6: 647–655. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.70019

article_title: Multiple Large Language Models' Performance on the Chinese Medical Licensing Examination: Quantitative Comparative Study.
citation: Diao Y, Wu M, Xu J, Pan Y. (2025). Multiple Large Language Models’ Performance on the Chinese Medical Licensing Examination: Quantitative Comparative Study. JMIR Human Factors. https://doi.org/10.2196/77978
title: NMLE Image Question Text Description Manual: physician-verified text descriptions of exam images and tables
description: A preprocessing artifact created to enable uniform text-only evaluation of six LLMs on the NMLE. Image-based questions were described using a template combining clinical standard terminology, visual key features, and diagnostic correlation information, without revealing answers. Descriptions were written independently by "2 attending physicians with more than 5 years of clinical experience," then cross-reviewed by a deputy chief physician; disagreements were settled by "3-person negotiation" to form the manual. Structured tables were converted to CSV format and diagrams into step-by-step textual explanations.
requirements: Descriptions generated by attending physicians with more than 5 years of clinical experience holding Chinese physician qualification certificates
Cross-review by a deputy chief physician from clinical imaging diagnosis
constraints: Text descriptions lost critical visual details from medical images, such as chest x-ray infiltrate density and blood smear leukocyte patterns
target_learning_goals: standardized evaluation of AI models on medical assessment questions
examples: Chest x-ray images were described with a template stating the examination type, visual features, anatomical location, and associated clinical information without direct diagnostic conclusions
key_sources: Diao Y, Wu M, Xu J, Pan Y. (2025). Multiple Large Language Models’ Performance on the Chinese Medical Licensing Examination: Quantitative Comparative Study. JMIR Human Factors. https://doi.org/10.2196/77978

article_title: The relationship between the nomophobic levels of higher education students in Ghana and academic achievement.
citation: Essel Harry Barton, Vlachopoulos Dimitrios, Tachie-Menson Akosua. (2021). The relationship between the nomophobic levels of higher education students in Ghana and their academic achievement. PLoS ONE 16(6): e0252880. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0252880
title: Nomophobia Questionnaire (NMP-Q), 20-item self-report scale with four latent constructs
description: The NMP-Q is a self-report Likert scale validated by Yildirim and Correia that measures nomophobic behaviour (fear of separation from one's phone) via four latent constructs: not being able to communicate, losing connectedness, not being able to access information, and giving up convenience. Each dimension is rated on seven pointers from strongly disagree to strongly agree, yielding scores from 20 to 140 with banding for absent, mild, moderate, and severe nomophobia. In this study it was administered as a Google Forms e-Questionnaire and showed "an overall Cronbach’s alpha (and, McDonald’s omega) of α = .97 (ωt = .97)".
requirements: Scores 100–140 infer severe nomophobia, 60–99 moderate, 21–59 mild, and 20 absent, per the scale's banding used in the study
target_learning_goals: assessing nomophobia prevalence and its association with academic achievement
examples: The investigators customised the NMP-Q into an e-Questionnaire with Google Forms and distributed it via institutional email and SMS in a single-blind data collection
key_sources: Essel Harry Barton, Vlachopoulos Dimitrios, Tachie-Menson Akosua. (2021). The relationship between the nomophobic levels of higher education students in Ghana and their academic achievement. PLoS ONE 16(6): e0252880. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0252880
